extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates / graduate students and contest-oriented readers learning complex geometry and algebraic number theory
extracted.subtask_description: Introductory/expository treatment of divisors on Riemann surfaces, line bundles and their morphisms, and basic algebraic number theory (minimal polynomials, algebraic integers, number fields, norms/traces, rings of integers). Intended as learning material with definitions, propositions, examples and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisors (Definition 51.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X be a Riemann manifold; a divisor D on X is a function D : X → Z which is nonzero on a discrete set of points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalizes objects like formal products of (z−p) powers as integer-valued functions supported on discrete sets. Example: the formal object (z−i)^{-3}·(z−∞)^{-4} corresponds to the divisor taking −3 at i, −4 at ∞, and 0 elsewhere. (Includes 'Abuse of Notation' that a point p may denote the divisor taking value 1 at p and 0 elsewhere.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Point-as-divisor notation (Abuse of Notation 51.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a point p ∈ X, write p to mean the divisor that takes value 1 at p and 0 elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enables writing formal sums like (−3)·i + (−4)·∞ to represent divisors; used throughout for compact notation and to translate formal products into divisor-valued functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of a divisor (Definition 51.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a divisor D on a compact surface X (so D has finite support), deg D := ∑_{p∈X} D(p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sum is finite because support is finite on compact X. Prototypical example: deg((−3)·i + (−4)·∞) = −7. Degree is a basic invariant used in Riemann–Roch and related statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisor of a meromorphic function / Principal divisor (Definition 51.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is meromorphic on a Riemann surface X, then the divisor of f, div(f), is defined by div(f)(p) = ord_p(f). Equivalently div(f) = ∑_p ord_p(f)·p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If D = div(f) for some f, D is called a principal divisor (analogy with principal ideal). Example: div((z−3)^2/(z−i)) = 2·3 + (−1)·i + (−1)·∞ (degree 0). The formalism lets one treat zeros and poles uniformly as integers at points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal divisors have degree zero (Proposition 51.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a divisor D on a compact surface X is principal (D = div(f) for some meromorphic f), then deg D = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used frequently as a constraint on possible principal divisors; essential input for Riemann–Roch and related counting arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial ordering of divisors (Definition 51.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write D ≥ 0 if D(p) ≥ 0 for all p ∈ X. For two divisors D1 and D2, write D1 ≥ D2 if D1 − D2 ≥ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pointwise ordering is used to formalize containment of allowed poles/zeros and to define spaces of functions with bounded poles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space L(D) of meromorphic functions bounded by D (Definition 51.4.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a divisor D on X, L(D) = { f meromorphic on X | div(f) ≥ −D }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interprets divisors as bounds on poles: f ∈ L(D) iff poles of f occur only where permitted by D and with order ≤ the coefficients of D. Exercises note monotonicity (D1 ≤ D2 ⇒ L(D1) ⊆ L(D2)), and for compact X: L(0) ≅ C and if deg D < 0 then L(D) = {0}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann–Roch theorem (Theorem 51.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let D be a divisor on an algebraic curve X of genus g, and K a canonical divisor on X. Then dim L(D) − dim L(K − D) = deg(D) + 1 − g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fundamental formula relating dimensions of spaces of sections with degree and genus. The text also prompts to 'Explain canonical divisor' and 'List some applications', indicating canonical divisor and applications are important explanatory/rubric aspects when presenting Riemann–Roch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line bundle (Definition 52.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A line bundle L over X is a set with a projection π : L → X, an open cover {U_i} of X, and for each U a chart ϕ : π^{-1}(U) → C × U that bijectively maps each fiber π^{-1}(p) to C × p; transition maps between charts restrict to C-vector space isomorphisms on fibers with analytic scaling factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights the combined analytic and 1-dimensional vector-space structure on each fiber; transition functions must be linear in the fiber coordinate and analytic on base. Guidance discusses intuition: think of a line bundle as 'graph paper' that can be twisted (nontrivial bundles like Möbius strip) and notes products of line bundles 'add twists'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sections of a line bundle (Definition 52.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A section on an open set U is a map f : U → L with π∘f = id_U. A global section is f : X → L. A section is analytic if in every local chart ϕ the coordinate map ϕ∘f|_{U1} : U1 → C×U1 is analytic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections generalize functions (graphs); the notion of analytic section corresponds to sections of the sheaf of analytic functions in other texts. Visual intuition: sections look like functions on the 'grid' given by the charts, but bundles may be nontrivial so a section need not be representable by a single global function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual criteria: trivial vs nontrivial line bundles (example and warning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trivial bundle looks like C × X with standard grid; nontrivial bundles arise by using transition charts that rescale fiber coordinates (e.g. scaling by z on patches of the Riemann sphere) and may produce twists (Möbius-strip-like phenomena).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns about over-relying on real-picture intuition (complex bundles are higher-dimensional). It gives the welding/scaling example on the Riemann sphere producing a nontrivial bundle and instructs the reader to check transition functions algebraically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line bundle morphism (Definition 52.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A map α : L1 → L2 between line bundles over the same base X satisfying π2∘α = π1 and such that in local charts the map has form (s,p) ↦ (f(p)·s, p) where f is analytic on the overlap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, α maps each fiber to the corresponding fiber and sends analytic sections to analytic sections. Exercise notes that f(p) must be nonzero on overlaps (otherwise invertibility fails). Example provided: α(y,x) = (y·x^2,x) is a homomorphism but not an isomorphism (kills fiber over 0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Isomorphism of line bundles (Definition 52.4.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two line bundles L1 and L2 are isomorphic if there exist line bundle morphisms α : L1 → L2 and β : L2 → L1 that are inverses of each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard notion: isomorphism must respect both fiber linear structure and analytic structure; checking local transition functions is the usual method to verify isomorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal polynomial (definition & properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: For α ∈ C, a minimal polynomial P(x) over Q is a monic polynomial with rational coefficients of smallest degree such that P(α) = 0. Its degree is the degree of α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimal polynomial is unique and irreducible over Q; any polynomial A(x) with A(α)=0 is divisible by the minimal polynomial. Roots of the minimal polynomial are the Galois conjugates of α (used throughout algebraic number theory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic number (Definition 53.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: An algebraic number is any α ∈ C which is a root of some polynomial with coefficients in Q. Denoted by Q̄ in the text (set of algebraic numbers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark that one can equivalently use polynomials in Z[x], since polynomials in Q[x] can be scaled to Z[x].

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic integer (Definition 53.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: An algebraic integer is an algebraic number whose minimal polynomial has integer coefficients (i.e., is a monic polynomial in Z[x]). The set of algebraic integers is denoted by Z̄ in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gauss's lemma implies that being a root of any monic integer polynomial suffices (no need to check minimality). Examples include integers, i, √2, primitive p-th roots of unity, etc. Rational numbers that are algebraic integers are exactly the ordinary integers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational algebraic integers are ordinary integers (Proposition 53.2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Z̄ ∩ Q = Z, i.e., a rational algebraic integer must be a (usual) integer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument sketch: if α∈Q is a root of a monic integer polynomial, rational root theorem implies α∈Z. Use as a simple but important structural constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic integers form a ring; algebraic numbers form a field (Proposition 53.2.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of algebraic integers is closed under addition and multiplication (a ring). The set of algebraic numbers is a field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes that the results will be justified later but are taken as known facts to be used in exercises/problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number field (Definition 53.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A number field K is a field containing Q as a subfield that is finite-dimensional as a Q-vector space; the degree of K is its dimension over Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Q(√2) with basis {1,√2} has degree 2. Non-examples: R and C are not number fields as they are infinite-dimensional over Q. Many later constructions (norm, trace, ring of integers) are defined relative to a number field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primitive element theorem (Artin's theorem 53.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every number field K is isomorphic to Q(α) for some algebraic number α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful structural result: any finite extension is generated by a single element; proof deferred to later problems. Prototypical example: Q(√3,√5) ≅ Q(√3 + √5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugates; Norm and Trace (Definitions 54.1.1, 54.1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For α algebraic of degree m with minimal polynomial, the m roots of that polynomial are the (Galois) conjugates. For α∈K with deg α = n and deg K = kn, define NK/Q(α) := ∏_{(Galois conj of α)} (conj)^{k} and TrK/Q(α) := k·∑_{(Galois conj of α)} (conj).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: k is the corrective multiplicity factor equal to deg K / deg α so norms/traces reflect the ambient field K. Examples show familiar formulas (e.g., for a+b√2, norm = a^2 − 2b^2, trace = 2a). Alternative viewpoint via embeddings into C: product/sum over embeddings. Norm is multiplicative, trace additive. Theorem 54.1.10 reframes norm as determinant of multiplication-by-α map µ_α and trace as its linear-algebra trace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norm and trace via linear algebra (Theorem 54.1.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: For K a number field and α∈K, let µ_α : K → K be multiplication by α viewed as a Q-linear map. Then NK/Q(α) = det(µ_α) and TrK/Q(α) = Tr(µ_α).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition explains multiplicativity/additivity and basis-independence; explicit matrix computations for examples (e.g., a+b√2) demonstrate formulas for det and trace. Proof splits into k=1 and k>1 cases with block-matrix argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norms and traces of algebraic integers are rational integers (Proposition 54.1.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If α is an algebraic integer, then NK/Q(α) and TrK/Q(α) are rational integers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vieta-formula style argument (or embedding argument) shows coefficients of minimal polynomial are integers; hence symmetric polynomials (norm/trace) are integers. Important when relating algebraic integers to arithmetic in number fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ring of integers OK (Definition 54.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a number field K, OK := K ∩ Z̄ is the ring of integers of K (the algebraic integers contained in K).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OK generalizes Z to number fields; examples for quadratic fields are given: if K = Q(√d) then OK is either Z[√d] or Z[(1+√d)/2] depending on d mod 4, with worked examples for d = 3 and d = 5. OK plays a central role in arithmetic of K (ideals, factorization, class groups, etc.).
